$comment: Apogee's scenario pool. Owned here: nothing reads a benchmark file to find out what a season is made of. A scenario is identified by the exact name KovaaK's uses, because that is what the player launches and what the leaderboard is keyed on. Edit this file to change the pool, then re-run sample:leaderboards and build:season. npm run validate:pool holds it to every claim made below.
$windows: A window is a difficulty band, and a scenario's band is the hardest tier any source publishes it in - see `bands`. Hardest rather than first, because a scenario Voltaic calls Intermediate and snakbox calls Hard is being asked for more by snakbox, and the ladder has to grade it at the harder ask or the rank it sets is one anybody in the harder band already holds. The previous pool placed each scenario by hand and the placement was a sentence in this comment rather than a rule; validate:pool now derives the window from `bands` and refuses a variant that disagrees with it.

ladder.$comment: Percentiles from the top of each scenario's KovaaK's leaderboard, one per rank, easiest first. They must fall from the first rank to the last, across the window handovers as well as inside a window. A family is graded on the best of its variants, so a player holds the highest rank any window gives them - and a rank whose percentile is not below every rank above it is reached by nobody, because whoever reaches it reaches a higher one at the same time. Letting a handover step back is the mistake this file keeps making. The cut before this one opened Intermediate at 44.9% where Novice closed at 43.8%, and repeated Advanced's four numbers verbatim for Expert, which left ranks 13 to 16 unreachable by construction. The cut before THAT had the same fault at two handovers. npm run distribution is what catches it: it sweeps the population through the real engine and names every rank nobody holds. This ladder is checked against it and skips none. The step back is not imaginary - a player does sit at a worse percentile on a harder board, so the same ability is a larger share there - but the sweep grades a player at one percentile on every board and cannot see it. Measuring the real step needs Apogee's own population, which is season 2's job. Until then the ladder descends. The cut before this one was also far too loose, which is a different fault and was found by playing it: a high-intermediate player topped out at rank 12 - the ceiling of Advanced - on 17 of the 22 families, and reached rank 15 on one. Sixteen ranks that a mid-ladder player finishes are sixteen ranks that mean nothing. What was wrong was the range, not the shape. A KovaaK's board is mostly people who played a scenario once, so a share of it is a much weaker claim than it sounds, and the old ladder ended at the top 1.4% - which npm run calibrate places at Voltaic's Nova, three ranks short of its last. Its whole Advanced window, 32% to 15%, sat inside Voltaic's *Intermediate*. This cut is anchored on the two references that survive conversion: Voltaic S5 holds a 1.1x to 2.2x spread across scenarios at each of its thresholds and Aimerz+ S1 a 1.2x to 2.2x across its Easy tier, tight enough that both really are percentile ladders in disguise, and both land their last rank at the top 0.1%. The sixteen below are the geometric mean of those two curves, read at sixteen evenly spaced positions along each. The same history that finished the old ladder now peaks at rank 12 with a median family at 9, which is what a high-intermediate player should read. Only the last window is not the reference's own shape. Both references end at the top 0.1%, and this pool cannot: validate:pool asks that seventy players sit above a window's hardest rank, the thinnest Expert board in the pool carries 9,878 entries, and 70/9,878 is the top 0.71%. So the last rank asks the top 0.8% - the limit with enough margin that a resample does not break it - and ranks 13 to 16 are spread geometrically from where Advanced closes. That is a real ceiling and not a preference: a finer cut than this would be a fact about fewer than seventy people. The four are close together in percentile and still a normal rank apart in score, because the top of a board is steep - about 2% of score per rank, which is what Voltaic's top ranks are worth too. Then the easy end was cut again, and the reason is a measurement this pool can make and the references cannot. The windows are stacked as one descending sequence on the theory that a harder scenario draws a stronger population, so the same player sits lower on its board. The corpus on this machine says that effect is small: the same history sits at a median top 10.0% across the Novice variants it has played, 12.9% across Intermediate, 13.0% across Advanced and 17.5% across Expert - under 2x from end to end, against a ladder that asked 86% at the bottom and 0.8% at the top. So the first eight ranks were not grading anybody. They closed at the top 22%, which that history cleared on every Novice scenario it had played and 13 of 15 Intermediate ones, most of them on one to five runs. The easy end is compressed to 86/72/56/42 and 31/22/15/10.5, which drops those 13 to 6. Ranks 13 to 16 are deliberately not touched: Air Voltaic's board saturates near the top - the whole top 2.2% of it spans ten points of score - so the four Expert ranks are already only 0.45% of score apart there, and a tighter cut puts a rank step under run-to-run noise. Maxing the Novice window is not a fault this can fix and is not trying to: a window a decent player does not clear is a window that never hands over. ONE SEQUENCE, AND WINDOWS THAT OVERLAP. The numbers used to be stored as one array per window, which is four chances to let a handover step back and the mistake this file kept making. They are stored as the sixteen now, because that is what they always were: a window's ladder is a slice of it, so a handover cannot step back by construction and the check that it descends is a check on one list. The slice is wider than the window's stride. Window w grades ranks 4w+1 through 4w+6, so Intermediate grades ranks 5 to 10 and can award a rank Advanced also awards. Abutting windows put a cliff at every handover: a player on the Intermediate scenarios topped out at rank 8 however well they played, and the ninth rank could only be had by launching a scenario they had never opened. Three cliffs up a sixteen-rank ladder, each landing where somebody is most likely to stop. The overlap costs nothing in grading - a family takes the best of its variants, so the harder scenario simply starts paying better at some point and the player crosses over when it does - and `src/core/season/windows.ts` owns the arithmetic so nothing has to rederive it. The top window is short by the overlap because it has nothing above to reach into. THE NOVICE WINDOW: EASY SCENARIO, HARD STANDARD. Ranks 1 to 6 were re-cut from 86/72/56/42/31/22 to 86/66/49/36/26/18, and the Novice rungs were swapped down to entry cuts their own sheets band Novice. The two changes are one idea and only work together. A beginner should be able to load the first scenario of a category without being beaten by the scenario itself, so the test at the bottom is now the easiest cut of its lineage rather than an Intermediate one - twenty of the Novice rungs were banded Intermediate or harder, which is the two-rank re-pitch showing up in the one window where it is wrong. The difficulty moves into the threshold instead: topping the Novice band now asks the top 18% of that scenario's board rather than the top 22%, and ranks 2 to 5 tighten by about a fifth each. Rank 1 is deliberately untouched at 86% - it is the on-ramp, and a ladder whose first rung is an achievement has no first rung. WHY 18% AND NOT LOWER. Rank 7 sits at 15% and belongs to the Intermediate window, which also grades ranks 5 and 6 through the overlap, so the whole sixteen must keep descending on one board. 18% leaves a three-point step to rank 7; 17% leaves two, which a resample can close. Asking more than that at the top of Novice means moving rank 7 and everything above it, which is a different change to a different window. The easier boards do carry a weaker population - the corpus sits at a median top 10.0% across Novice variants against 17.5% across Expert - so a tighter percentile at this end is measuring the same ability the old numbers did, not a harder one. Rank 2 is 66% and not the 63% the geometric fit wanted, because 63% left Evasive Switching's second rank held by nobody: npm run distribution sweeps the population and reported it, three points of slack closed it, and that is the whole reason for the odd number. Every Novice rung is cut from this ladder now rather than adopted - `cut:thresholds --over-adopted --window 0` - because an entry benchmark's own tiers are pitched at a beginner too, and adopting both the easy scenario and the easy tier is how a bottom band ends up asking nothing. Windows 1 to 3 still take a published tier where one exists.

$matchWindow: Which window a ranked match draws its three scenarios from. Intermediate: novice scenarios stop separating two players who can both max them, and expert ones ask a first-week player to play something they cannot score on at all.
$subCategories: Eleven, derived rather than chosen: data/subskills.json normalises the category names all 43 committed benchmarks publish for their own scenarios and counts how many name each one. Nine are Voltaic's, and the derivation reproduces Voltaic's published mapping on all 106 of their scenarios, which is what makes the same treatment of everybody else's believable. Two are not Voltaic's and are named by benchmarks their sheet cannot see: Micro Clicking by eight, Reading Tracking by seven. Named in two words the way snakbox, Avasive, wobin and Aimerz+ name them, rather than as the bare word, because the bare word does not survive being read on its own - 'Micro' and 'Speed' mean different things in different categories, and a weakness map or a queue name showing one word cannot say which. Regenerate with npm run build:subskills; do not hand-edit either file's classification.
$sources: Every benchmark the pool may draw a scenario from, and nothing else. This replaces the old rule - 'the fifteen most-played benchmarks on evxl' - which could not reach Viscose, Jade Palace, Lemon Static or snakbox however good their scenarios are, and let in nothing from outside the list however good it is. Each of these is a benchmark evxl lists, has a committed definition under data/benchmarks/, and contributes at least one scenario; validate:pool checks all three. WHY IT GREW FROM 23 TO 31. The six-category rebuild picks families by hand from the whole of KovaaK's, and the eight added here are simply the committed sheets those picks turned out to rest on - TSK Mixed alone grades sixteen of them. Every one was already sitting in data/benchmarks/ and in the evxl registry; none of them is new evidence, and leaving them unnamed only meant the pool was drawing on sheets it would not admit to. TWO ABSENCES ARE STILL DELIBERATE. Avasive S2 is not here because it cannot be: its 96 scenarios carry 26 leaderboard entries between the largest of them, so no percentile cut from one of its boards describes anything. The pool does use two Avasive scenarios, and they are admitted on a written reason rather than on Avasive's authority - which is the honest way round, because what recommends them is the shape of the test and not the sheet's grading. e1se Tracking Routine is not here because it is a routine rather than a graded ladder - its 'Intermediate' tier holds Voltaic Novice scenarios, and banding by it would drag the easiest scenarios in the pool two windows up.
$bands: Which window each source's difficulty tiers belong to. One row per tier rather than one per scenario, because a tier is what its author graded as a unit and 76 hand placements is 76 chances to put a Novice scenario in the Expert band - which samples fine, builds fine, and produces four top ranks anybody clears in one run. The two judgements worth naming: Voltaic's Elite tier is window 3 but is never used, because every Elite board is under 5,000 entries and a rank cut from the top 1.4% of one would be whatever two players happened to score; and Aimerz+, Revosect S1, Jade Palace and snakbox's hardest tiers are read as sitting above Voltaic's Advanced, which is the one claim here their authors did not make. npm run distribution is what checks it - a band placed too high leaves ranks nobody holds. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT BANDED. Two of the sheets the pool now names carry no difficulty to band by, and inventing one for them would be the exact mistake the paragraph above is about. TSK Mixed Benchmarks names its ten tiers after categories - Static, Strafes, Reactive by slapped - so 'Static' says what a scenario trains and nothing about how hard it is. cA Static S1 has one tier called All. Aimerz+ Static Clicking also has one tier, but it is called Hard, which IS difficulty and is banded. A scenario no tier can place declares its own window instead, and what protects the ladder there is the ascent check: within a family, a rung banded harder may not sit below a rung banded easier. That is a check on the order the author chose rather than on each rung matching a number somebody else published, which is what a season that deliberately re-pitches two ranks harder needs.

1w2ts Pasu Perfected.why: Micro Clicking, which this season does not cut as its own category. Lemon files it under Micro and Viscose under Precision - the same scenario, two names, neither of them a category here. Micro clicking is static clicking on small targets: the same mechanic at a smaller scale rather than a different one, so Static Clicking is the parent it belongs to. The family is called Micro precisely so the distinction is not lost inside it.

The final two variants make incomplete contact costly instead of relying only on smaller Elite bots. They deliberately retain two useful Voltaic variants rather than an entire stock four-rung family. Cross-author handovers and regeneration difficulty need playtesting.

$subCategoryOverrides: Scenarios where the pool's sub-skill deliberately disagrees with the one derived from the benchmark sheets, and why. WHY THERE ARE ANY. The corpus names eleven sub-skills and this season grades six, so five have no category to sit in: Micro Clicking, Linear Clicking, Control Tracking, Reading Tracking and Stability Switching. A scenario the sheets file under one of those is not miscategorised - it is being graded at the resolution this season cut, and it has to land in the nearest sub-skill that exists. Every entry below says which unrepresented sub-skill it came from and why its home is the right one, because 'the season has no category for it' explains that an override is needed and not that this override is correct. Season 2 can cut finer and these go away; validate:pool fails an override that has come to agree with the derivation, so they cannot outlive their reason.
$families: Static Clicking is preserved. Five non-static circuits each contain six families and four bands. The weakness-specific theory pass replaces seven families; data/benchmark_theory.json records source coverage and the new scenario identities. Band handovers and enjoyment remain playtest judgements.

$familyNotes: Why a family's scenarios are what they are, where the choice needed defending. Written on the family rather than on a variant's `source` because the two are different claims: `source` says where a NUMBER came from and is rewritten whenever the thresholds are re-cut, so a reason parked there does not survive npm run cut:thresholds. Static Clicking.headline: Still targets. Time between kills.
Static Clicking.description: Targets stationary. Score = gap between kills. One large initial flick → one small micro-correction → click. Straight line target to target, no overflick. During micro, next target already located in peripheral.

Dynamic Clicking.headline: Read. Confirm. Commit.
Dynamic Clicking.description: Follow the movement into each shot. Read arcs beyond the apex and stay with multi-hit targets until the final click. Smooth transitions make the next target easier to read.

Precise Tracking.headline: Stay connected.
Precise Tracking.description: Match the target through horizontal strafes, vertical travel and changing paths. Make clean corrections when contact breaks. Use an easier cut when you lose the movement; difficulty should leave room to learn.

Reactive Tracking.headline: React, recover, settle.
Reactive Tracking.description: Watch the target, react to the change, then match its new movement. Stops and teleports join ground and air reads. If you start guessing turns or forcing the mouse, step down and rebuild clean contact.

Speed Switching.headline: Find pace. Keep precision.
Speed Switching.description: Hold fire, land close and finish each target before transferring. Mix compact flicks, wide routes and shrinking targets. In practice, try a short speed burst on an easier cut; use complete runs for benchmark scores.

Evasive Switching.headline: Earn every transfer.
Evasive Switching.description: Flick in, match the movement and confirm the kill. Read the next target without abandoning this one. Regeneration tests clean finishes; varied arcs and strafes keep the task about reading, not memorising turns.
